issues.legal_issue: A statutory appeal that is reviewable by constitutional courts does not necessarily require a personal hearing, and omission of a speaking order does not invariably require the appeal to be set aside or remitted.
material_facts: The appellant’s statutory appeal was dismissed by the State Government without a personal hearing or a reasoned order.
The dispute could be decided on points of law, and no determination or adjudication of facts was involved.
The High Court examined the relevant legal questions and declined to set aside the State Government’s decision or remit the appeal.
issues.conclusion: The State Government was not required to give a personal hearing. It ought to have issued a speaking order, but the omission did not justify setting aside the decision or remitting the appeal in this case.
issues.legal_principle: A personal hearing is not invariably required in disposing of a statutory appeal. Where an order may be challenged under Articles 226 or 227 of the Constitution, courts ordinarily insist on a speaking order giving reasons; however, a non-speaking order is not invalid in every case, and remittal is not necessary where no factual determination is involved and the reviewing court can examine the legal issues.

predicates.statutory_appeal_reviewed_by_constitutio: A party pursued a statutory appeal whose decision was challenged before a constitutional court.
predicates.non_speaking_order: The authority disposed of the appeal without giving reasons for its decision.
predicates.no_factual_determination_required: The dispute required no determination or adjudication of facts.

issues.definition: When a statutory appeal is reviewed by a constitutional court, the authority gives no reasons, and no factual determination is needed, a personal hearing is not required and remittal is not required solely because the order is non-speaking.

issues.legal_issue: A party cannot disown a tenancy or advance a position on the applicability of tenancy law that contradicts the position it consistently maintained in earlier proceedings.
material_facts: The appellant had repeatedly treated the other party as his tenant and had pursued proceedings to terminate the tenancy and recover possession.
In earlier proceedings, the appellant had expressly maintained that the land was not service land and that tenancy law applied.
The other party had long been in cultivating possession and had paid rent to the appellant.
The appellant later argued that the land was service land, that tenancy law did not apply, and that the other party was not a tenant.
issues.conclusion: The appellant could not change his position and contend that tenancy law did not apply or that the other party was not his tenant; the other party’s possession and payment of rent were as a tenant.
issues.legal_principle: A litigant cannot shift to a position contrary to the case maintained throughout prior proceedings. Cultivating possession and payment of rent to the landholder supported the conclusion that the person was in possession as a tenant. The Court did not accept the appellant’s attempt to characterize his earlier tenancy proceedings as lacking jurisdiction on the basis of his newly advanced position.

predicates.challenge_to_tenancy_status_after_prior_: A party challenged the other person’s tenancy status after previously pursuing proceedings treating that person as a tenant.
predicates.inconsistent_litigation_position: The party advanced a position that contradicted the position it had maintained in earlier proceedings.
predicates.cultivating_possession_with_rent_paid: The other person cultivated the land and paid rent to the party claiming to be the landholder.

issues.definition: If a party challenges tenancy status after earlier tenancy proceedings, takes a contradictory litigation position, and the other person cultivated the land and paid rent, the party cannot disown the tenancy.

issues.legal_issue: Service of a notice terminating a tenancy and filing an application for possession do not end the tenancy before possession is ordered, so a tenant who remains in possession at vesting can acquire occupant rights under the abolition law.
material_facts: The appellant served a notice purporting to terminate the tenancy and applied for possession under the tenancy law.
The application for possession was not granted before the land vested in the State.
The other party remained in possession as a tenant when the land vested.
The abolition law granted occupant rights to a qualifying person in possession at vesting.
issues.conclusion: The tenancy had not ended merely through service of notice and filing the possession application; because the tenant remained in possession at vesting, the tenant acquired the rights of an occupant.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 44(1) and 32(2) of the Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Land Act, 1950, notice and an application for possession do not by themselves terminate the tenancy; the process is not complete until possession is ordered by the competent authority. Rule 28(5) provides that, upon the application for possession being granted, termination takes effect from the commencement of the following year. Accordingly, a tenant still in possession at vesting may acquire occupant rights under section 6(1) of the Hyderabad Abolition of Inams and Cash Grants Act, 1954. The Court doubted the contrary view of the Bombay High Court Full Bench in Dattatraya Sadashiv Dhond v. Ganpati Raghu Gaoli, 67 Bombay Law Reporter 521.

rule.if: proceeding_concerning_occupant_rights_on_vesting and termination_notice_served and possession_application_filed and no_possession_order_before_vesting and tenant_in_possession_at_vesting

predicates.proceeding_concerning_occupant_rights_on: The proceeding determines whether a person acquired occupant rights when land vested under an abolition law.
predicates.termination_notice_served: The landholder served a notice purporting to terminate the tenancy.
predicates.possession_application_filed: The landholder applied to the competent authority for possession of the land.
predicates.no_possession_order_before_vesting: The competent authority had not ordered possession in favour of the landholder before the land vested.
predicates.tenant_in_possession_at_vesting: The tenant remained in possession of the land when vesting occurred.

issues.definition: In a proceeding about occupant rights on vesting, a tenant who remains in possession when the land vests acquires occupant rights if the landholder has served a termination notice and filed a possession application but has obtained no possession order before vesting.

issues.legal_issue: An issue directly and substantially decided in an earlier proceeding between the parties cannot be relitigated in a later proceeding.
material_facts: In an earlier proceeding, the High Court dismissed the appellant’s challenge after deciding that the other party had acquired occupant rights upon abolition and vesting.
That issue was directly and substantially in dispute in the earlier proceeding.
The appellant sought to contest the same occupant-rights issue again in the later proceeding.
issues.conclusion: The question whether the other party had acquired occupant rights was barred by res judicata and could not be re-agitated.
issues.legal_principle: The principles of res judicata prevent re-agitation of an issue that directly and substantially fell for determination and was decided against a party in an earlier proceeding. The Court applied those principles to the earlier High Court decision concerning acquisition of occupant rights.

predicates.later_proceeding_repeats_issue: A party raised in a later proceeding an issue that had been raised in an earlier proceeding.
predicates.same_issue_directly_and_substantially_de: The same issue directly and substantially arose in the earlier proceeding and was decided against that party.

issues.definition: When a later proceeding repeats an issue that was directly and substantially decided against the party in an earlier proceeding, that issue cannot be relitigated.
